The classic Koh Samui scam is a damage claim after a jet-ski or scooter rental: film the vehicle from every angle before you ride and never leave your passport as a deposit. The other common traps are taxis that quote double (agree the fare before you get in), paid look-alike TDAC websites (the official one at tdac.immigration.go.th is free) and card terminals or ATMs that offer to charge you in your home currency (always choose THB). If something goes wrong, call the Tourist Police on 1155.

Good to know: Koh Samui is not a dangerous island, and most people you deal with are honest. Scams here are mostly about money, not violence, and nearly all of them can be avoided with a phone camera, a written price and a refusal to hand over your passport. Last checked November 2026.

Jet-ski damage claims

How it works

You rent a jet ski by the hour on a busy beach, usually Chaweng or Lamai. When you bring it back, the operator points to a scratch, crack or dent and says you caused it. The demand can be anything from a few thousand to tens of thousands of baht. If you left your passport as a deposit, they keep it until you pay. Threats and groups of "friends" turning up are part of the pressure. The UK government's travel advice specifically warns against handing your passport to jet-ski rental businesses.

How to avoid it

  • Before you ride, film the whole jet ski slowly, including the hull below the waterline, with the operator in shot. Do the same when you return.
  • Ask for a written rental agreement with the price, time and what happens if there is damage.
  • Never leave your passport. Offer a photocopy and a cash deposit, or walk away.
  • Check whether your travel insurance covers jet skis at all; many policies don't.
  • Better still, take a guided trip with a licensed operator, where the guide handles the paperwork and the route. Our Jet Ski Safari to Pig Island costs 9,950 THB per jet ski, with a guide, safety briefing and agreed terms in writing.

What to do if it happens

Stay calm and don't hand over cash under pressure. Call the Tourist Police on 1155 and ask them to attend; they deal with these disputes regularly. Show your before-and-after video. If you must pay to get your passport back, get a written receipt and report it to the Tourist Police afterwards. More on safe riding is in our Koh Samui jet ski guide.

Scooter damage and passport deposits

The scooter version works the same way: the shop holds your passport, and at return it finds damage that may have been there before. Shops that keep passports have all the bargaining power.

  • Leave a cash deposit instead (commonly a few thousand baht) and get a receipt. Never leave your passport, as the UK government advises.
  • Photograph and video every panel, the tyres, the mirrors and the fuel gauge before you ride off, with the shop owner present.
  • Check the bike works: brakes, lights, horn, and a helmet that fits.
  • Ride with a licence valid for motorcycles (an IDP with the motorcycle category plus your home licence). Without it, police can fine you and your insurance probably won't pay after a crash.
  • Be aware that many rental scooters in tourist areas are not properly registered or insured.

Our Koh Samui motorbike rental guide covers prices, licences and helmet fines (up to 2,000 THB).

Taxi overcharging

Samui's red-and-yellow taxis have meters, but drivers almost never use them. Fares are negotiated and are high by Thai standards, especially late at night, in the rain and from the piers.

  • Agree the full price before you get in, and confirm whether it is per car or per person.
  • At Samui Airport, use the official taxi and minivan counters in the arrivals area, which display fixed prices by zone.
  • Grab works on Samui, best in Chaweng, Bophut and Lamai and weaker on the west coast. Waits of 5–20 minutes are normal, with surge pricing in rain and at night. The price is fixed in the app.
  • Songthaews (shared pickup trucks) along the ring road are the cheapest option in the daytime; confirm the price before getting on, especially after dark, when they work as private taxis.
  • Ask your hotel what a fair fare is before you go out.
  • If a driver raises the price mid-journey or refuses to stop, photograph the number plate and call the Tourist Police on 1155.

See getting around Koh Samui and Samui Airport for typical fares.

Fake TDAC and visa websites

Every foreign visitor must file the Thailand Digital Arrival Card (TDAC) within 3 days before arriving. The official site, tdac.immigration.go.th, is free. In March 2026, Thai immigration said at least 10% of foreign arrivals had used look-alike sites, some charging fees and harvesting passport data. Search ads often push these sites to the top.

  • Type the address yourself: tdac.immigration.go.th. Government sites end in .go.th.
  • If a site asks for a card payment for the TDAC, it is not the official one.
  • Visa applications go through thaievisa.go.th. Agencies on other domains charge extra and some are scams.
  • No "Thailand tourist entry fee" is being collected as of November 2026. Ignore any site asking you to pre-pay one.

Full entry rules are in our Thailand visa guide.

Card skimming and DCC

When an ATM or a card machine asks whether to charge you in your home currency or in Thai baht, always choose THB. The "home currency" option is called dynamic currency conversion, and the exchange rate it uses is usually several percent worse than your bank's. Some shop and restaurant staff choose it for you, so check the screen before you tap or enter your PIN.

  • Use ATMs inside bank branches or shopping malls rather than stand-alone machines on dark streets. The UK government notes incidents of ATM skimming in Thailand.
  • Cover the keypad when you enter your PIN, and keep your card in sight when you pay.
  • Foreign cards pay a 220–250 THB fee at most Thai ATMs (150 THB at AEON machines), so withdraw larger amounts less often.
  • Turn on transaction alerts in your banking app.

Our banks and money guide has the full ATM fee table.

Ticket touts and fake tours

Muay Thai seats

Touts with loudspeaker trucks and street stalls sell "VIP" fight tickets at inflated prices. Buy at the stadium box office, where the prices are posted. See Muay Thai fight nights on Koh Samui.

Full Moon "entry tickets"

The Full Moon Party on Koh Phangan charges an entry fee of about 200 THB, paid at the gate on Haad Rin. Nobody on Samui can sell you a valid advance "entry ticket". We sell return boat transfers only: the Full Moon Party speedboat from Koh Samui costs 1,400 THB, and the entry fee is paid on the night. Avoid unlicensed boats and minivans on party nights; the UK government links them to assaults and accidents.

Closed attractions sold as open

Ang Thong National Marine Park closes every year from 1 November to 15 December and reopens on 16 December. Anyone selling an "Ang Thong" trip for those dates is either taking you somewhere else or won't sail. Check our Ang Thong Marine Park guide for dates. Pig Island runs all year.

Elephant riding

Some camps advertise "sanctuary" or "eco" visits but still offer rides, bathing or shows. Ask directly whether riding or bathing is offered; a genuine sanctuary will say no. See our elephant sanctuary guide.

Job offers and online rentals

The UK government warns about job offers in Southeast Asia that seem too good to be true, which can lead to people being held and forced to work in scam centres. Be equally careful with villa rentals advertised on social media: never pay a deposit by bank transfer to a stranger for a property you haven't seen or can't verify.

Fake hotel and tour pages

In May 2025 the Tourist Police Bureau arrested three people who had set up Facebook pages copying well-known hotels, advertised fake promotions and took more than 20,000 US dollars from travellers who arrived to find no reservation. Police advise checking any hotel or tour page on social media carefully before you pay. Book through the business's own website, check that the page links back to it, and be wary of discounts that only work by bank transfer. A licensed tour company will give you its licence number; ours is TAT 43/01467.

Booking safely

  • Licensed agency: every tour seller in Thailand needs a tourism business licence. Ask for the number and check it on the Department of Tourism's online licence search. Ours is TAT licence 43/01467.
  • Secure payment in THB: pay by card through a secure checkout that charges in baht, so your bank, not a stranger, handles the exchange. Avoid cash deposits to someone on the beach.
  • Written cancellation policy: know before you pay what happens if the weather turns. On our day tours you get a full refund 48 hours or more before departure, 50% between 24 and 48 hours, and nothing under 24 hours or for a no-show. On Ang Thong tours it is a full refund 48 hours or more before departure. If we cancel for weather, you choose a full refund or a new date.
  • Clear inclusions: check whether hotel transfers, lunch and park fees are included. Our hotel pickup is included from most areas of Koh Samui; +400 THB per person return from Lipa Noi, Nathon, Bang Kao, Thong Krut and other remote areas. Cash island fees (Ang Thong 300 THB adult, Koh Madsum about 50 THB) are paid on the day.

The Pig Island speedboat tour (1,450 THB adult) is a good example of a straightforward, all-year trip with clear terms. Questions? [kp_wa]
